posts.cooked:
MarioFanaticXV:

Remember the days when instead of DLC, we had cheat codes for this kind of thing? I miss those days.

 

And none of us would be able to talk to eachother about it unless we happened to meet in person at some point?

And this game wouldn't even exist because it would have failed at the pitch stage or gotten taken over by people who turned it into a DC game, alterred it unrecognizable and made it suck and we wouldn't even know because it would be the only game like it in the stores?

Ah, the good old days.  When I played Battletech with hand drawn maps and slips of paper with mech names on it because all I could afford were the tech readout books, and I played by myself because I didn't know where to find a gaming community.

Actually, we had the internet and chatrooms in the 90s, and they had it even back in the 80s (thought admittedly, only those who were really into computers actually used it then). Not to mention they had phones, radio, and telegraph long before that. While telecommunications is fairly new in the scope of human history, it's not THAT new.

Besides, just because you can name something that got better with time (such as the internet) does not change the fact that other things have become worse (such as the way that video game developers treat their customers).

posts.name: Silverleaf
posts.cooked:
For me, arcades were something you only really got in touristy places, primarily seaside holiday towns. There wasn't one in my inland town as a kid (most pubs, etc, would have a slot machine or two and maybe an arcade game, but that's it).

But my grandmother lived just outside Skegness (a couple of hours drive away on the coast, very popular but somewhat downmarket Victorian seaside town), and that place is full of arcades. We used to visit her a lot, and I'd be given "spending money" for the week which inevitably ended up gone in two days, leaving me bored in the evenings when my parents and grandparents would sit in the pub doing boring adult things until someone took pity on me and gave me extra cash.

posts.name: MarioFanaticXV
posts.cooked: As much as I find the idea laughable now, it is important to note that back in the 80s and 90s, arcade cabinets were often much more powerful than the consoles and even most home computers of their age. This meant you could have much more visually attractive games in the arcade than you could produce for homes- which I believe is one of the major things that lead to the downfall of arcades, now that even indie games can look really "pretty".
